lessons.1: Imagine we're opening our online store for the very first time. Where does Java begin? Open `ShopApplication.java` and find `main()`: it hands the application to `SpringApplication.run()`. That's why this is Company 1—we need to know who turns the lights on before touring the rooms. Notice that this line starts the framework; it doesn't personally build every controller or service.
lessons.2: Our shop can start without telling us whether setup has finished. So how do we hear that Spring Boot is ready? Look at `@EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)` and the working-directory log inside `applicationReadyCode()`. We study this now to recognize lifecycle events. One subtle point: this is our lesson order, not runtime order; the ready event fires after Spring's configuration work.
lessons.3: Okay, we've seen how Spring Boot starts our application. But once Shopizer is running, customers and administrators send requests. Should those requests pass through unchecked? That's why we're opening `croseSiteFilter()`. Notice how it creates `XssFilter` and registers `/shop/**`, `/api/**`, and `/customer/**`. Think of this as a checkpoint at the shop entrance. We study the registration before response handling, but registering a filter doesn't by itself guarantee XSS protection.
lessons.4: Picture a customer asking our shop for product data. Java has objects, but the browser expects something like JSON. Who translates? Open `configureMessageConverters()` and watch the Jackson converter enter Spring MVC's list. We place this after request filtering because handling a request also means preparing its representation. Keep an eye on this override: replacing versus extending Spring's default converters matters in a real interview.
lessons.5: Suppose someone enters the shop's root URL: `/`. Do we need to write a whole controller just to show a page? See `addViewControllers()` set the view name to `shop`. This is Company 5 because you already know how HTTP data gets processed; now you can see how a URL leads to a view. The view name still needs a suitable resolver to become actual content.
lessons.6: Now the homepage route makes sense, but what about work that should happen around many requests—like changing language or handling cross-origin traffic? We shouldn't paste that code into every controller. Open `addInterceptors()` and follow the locale and CORS registrations, especially `/services/**` and `/api/**`. This comes after basic routing so you can compare MVC interceptors with servlet filters. The commented-out store-filter block is not active.
lessons.7: Imagine a customer downloading a product image. Would you squeeze JPEG bytes into the same explanation as a JSON order? Let's inspect `byteArrayHttpMessageConverter()`. It configures a converter for byte content and image media types. That's why we come here after Company 4: same HTTP response pipeline, very different payload. Watch the supported media types; they determine when this converter is suitable.
lessons.8: We registered a language-change interceptor in Company 6, but where does that interceptor object come from? Open `localeChangeInterceptor()` and see its factory method. Imagine a shopper switching the storefront language: the interceptor helps interpret that request. We're following the actual dependency of the earlier registration instead of introducing an unrelated feature. Next we'll see how Spring remembers the visitor's locale.
lessons.9: Company 6 also registers a component named `corsFilter()`. What really comes back from that method? Open it before assuming its name means it's a servlet filter. Follow the object created and used by `addInterceptor()`. This is the perfect moment to distinguish names from contracts: a thing passed to the MVC interceptor registry must support that job. We place this after the locale factory because both came from the same registration method.
lessons.10: A shopper changes language, then clicks another page. How does the shop know which locale to use next? Look at `localeResolver()` and the session-based resolver it configures. We study this after the language interceptor because recognizing a switch and remembering the choice are separate responsibilities. Think of one as listening to the request and the other as storing the preference for subsequent pages.
lessons.11: We know which language a visitor wants. But where do translated words such as button labels actually come from? Open `messageSource()` and notice the resource-bundle setup. We visit this after locale resolution so you can connect a locale with the translated messages it selects. Picking English or French is one step; loading the corresponding text from message files is another.
lessons.12: A message bundle exists, but real application code needs a convenient way to use it. Inspect the `messages()` bean and its helper object. This follows Company 11 because we first created the source of translations and now make it easier for other components to consume them. Imagine avoiding repetitive resource lookups across the storefront. Trace which bean is returned rather than inventing a hidden translation service.
lessons.13: Let's move from customer-facing language to settings. A real e-commerce app has configuration that shouldn't be scattered through Java literals. Open `mapper()` in `ShopizerPropertiesConfig.java` and inspect how property data is prepared. We study this after shared message setup because both are application-wide support features. Ask yourself which settings are loaded, how missing values behave, and who consumes the resulting object.
lessons.14: Imagine a task that takes longer than a normal web request. Should our customer stare at a frozen page while the server waits? Visit `getAsyncExecutor()` and see the executor used for background work. This comes after the basic web configuration because asynchronous execution is supporting infrastructure, not the entry-point request handler itself. Pay attention to capacity and thread naming before assuming background work is unlimited.
lessons.15: Starting background work is only half the story. What happens when a task fails and nobody is directly waiting for its result? Open `getAsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler()`. We put this immediately after the executor so the happy path and failure path are learned together. A mentor's rule here: if work moves off the request thread, you also need a deliberate plan for diagnosing errors.
lessons.16: Our controllers sometimes need information about the current shop or language without decoding it by hand. How is that supplied? Check `addArgumentResolvers()` in `WebConfig.java`. We study controller argument resolution after global setup because now we're getting close to actual handler parameters. The interesting part is the registration of custom resolvers—next we'll step into them and see how they decide which parameters to handle.
lessons.17: We registered a merchant-store argument resolver, but Spring can't give it every method parameter. How does it decide? Open `supportsParameter()` and examine the parameter type check. This comes immediately after Company 16 because registration means little unless we understand when the resolver activates. Think of it as checking the shipping label before accepting a parcel for the right destination.
lessons.18: Okay, the parameter is a merchant store. Now which store should a request receive—and how do we know the requester may use it? Read `resolveArgument()` in the same resolver. We placed it after `supportsParameter()` because detection must come before resolution in our mental model. Follow the lookup and authorization-related branches carefully: giving a controller the wrong store could become a serious multi-tenant data problem.
lessons.19: The store resolver makes sense. What if a controller instead asks for a `Language` parameter? Open the second `supportsParameter()`, this time in `LanguageArgumentResolver.java`. We learn the two resolvers side by side so you'll recognize the same Spring MVC contract applied to a different piece of context. The method answers 'Can I handle this parameter?'—it doesn't yet choose the language.
lessons.20: Now Spring knows a `Language` argument belongs to this resolver. Where does its value come from? Step into `resolveArgument()` in `LanguageArgumentResolver.java`. This follows Company 19 as the second half of the contract: first qualify the parameter, then supply its value. Connect this to our earlier locale lessons without assuming that language and locale are always the exact same object.
lessons.21: Before diving farther into request features, let's look at something easy to miss: the servlet container has its own lifecycle. Open `contextInitialized()` in `ShopServletContextListener.java` and see what it reports when the web context begins. We study this after argument resolution to widen our picture from individual requests to the application's host environment. A servlet listener is not the same thing as a controller.
lessons.22: A server doesn't only start—it shuts down too. What should happen to resources such as caches then? Examine `contextDestroyed()` and its cleanup. It's paired with Company 21 so startup and shutdown don't become unrelated trivia. Picture redeploying the store: leaving shared resources running can create leaks and confusing behavior. Watch what this actual method stops rather than assuming every resource is automatically cleaned up.
lessons.23: Developers building a storefront also need to understand its APIs. Can we document them without manually listing every endpoint on a website? Open the Swagger `api()` configuration and notice the Docket setup. We study it after request handling and lifecycle because the API is now meaningful. The documentation tool describes endpoints; it does not itself implement the business operations behind them.
lessons.24: Swagger has a Docket, but should it scan every Java package in the repository? Check `requestHandlers()` and its package-selection logic. This is the next company because Company 23 calls this helper while deciding which handlers to document. Imagine giving customers an API catalog full of internal-only controllers—that's why discovery rules deserve attention. Follow the exact packages in the original source.
lessons.25: An API catalog also needs a title and description. Where does that information come from? Open `apiInfo()` and inspect the metadata it provides. We place this after Swagger handler selection because documenting 'which endpoints' and explaining 'what this API is' are different jobs. The method builds descriptive information; it doesn't change which HTTP operations exist.
lessons.26: Product images often live somewhere other than the running application. Suppose the same shop is deployed locally and in the cloud: how do image locations differ? Open `img()` and follow the configuration choice. This comes after API documentation as we turn to another cross-cutting concern—resource storage. Check the real condition rather than assuming every Shopizer deployment uses the same location.
lessons.27: We're entering security now. When someone sends an authentication token, what component should inspect the request first? Open `authenticationTokenFilter()`. We begin the security sequence here because it gives you the filter that later authentication flows depend on. Think of the checkout door: recognizing a token at the entrance is not yet the same as deciding whether the shopper is authorized to buy.
lessons.28: The filter can inspect a token, but applications still need a service for working with credentials. See what `credentialsService()` exposes. We study this after the authentication filter to separate incoming-request inspection from the business rules around credentials. Try to identify the concrete implementation and how it is registered as a bean; knowing the interface name alone won't tell us its security guarantees.
lessons.29: Suppose the store saves a password. Should it keep the readable password in its database? Absolutely not. Find `passwordEncoder()` and see the BCrypt encoder bean. We place it after credential-service wiring because password verification needs a suitable hashing component. Remember: an encoder is not encryption you later reverse. We compare hashes, and real login code must call the encoder correctly.
lessons.30: Now imagine a valid user has just logged in. What should the application do next? Open `userAuthenticationSuccessHandler()`. This follows credential setup so we can distinguish verifying a login from responding after successful authentication. Check which handler object the factory returns. The important teaching point: a success callback is not where you should silently skip authorization checks.
lessons.31: Why would the services API need its own success handler instead of using the shop's browser behavior? Look at `servicesAuthenticationSuccessHandler()` and compare it with Company 30. We examine these factories consecutively because Shopizer has different kinds of clients. A browser session and a service integration may need different post-login handling even when both authenticate successfully.
lessons.32: We've met filters, encoders, and login callbacks. One more shared piece appears before the customer security adapter: `customerFacade()`. Open the factory and inspect the actual facade type. This position closes the outer security configuration's shared dependencies before we enter nested customer-specific rules. The facade may simplify customer operations, but it is not automatically an authentication provider just because security code creates it.
lessons.33: Let's enter the customer security adapter. Other components sometimes need an actual `AuthenticationManager`. Where is that bean exposed? Check `authenticationManagerBean()` in the customer adapter. This is our starting point inside that section because the manager coordinates authentication decisions. We separate obtaining the manager from configuring which users and requests it will handle.
lessons.34: Would you expect every resource, including certain static files or explicitly excluded paths, to pass through the same security filter chain? Examine the adapter's web-security `configure()` method. We study exclusions before private authorization rules so you can distinguish 'not in this filter chain' from 'permitted by an authorization rule.' That distinction becomes crucial when reviewing application exposure.
lessons.35: Security rules can't authenticate a person unless there is a way to load that person's details. Open the next `configure()` overload and find the customer user-details service. We place it after path exclusions because now we're defining how Shopizer recognizes a customer. Focus on the concrete service wired into authentication, not merely the overloaded method name.
lessons.36: Alright, we can find customer identities. Which URLs can they access, and what happens during logout? Walk through the HttpSecurity `configure()` chain. This is the right moment to read access rules as a complete story: anonymous requests, authenticated shoppers, and session termination. One permissive-looking matcher can change the whole shop's security posture, so don't judge the chain from a single line.
lessons.37: Company 36 refers to a Basic-auth entry point. What creates that entry point, and what response does it prepare for an unauthenticated browser? Open `shopAuthenticationEntryPoint()`. We're following a dependency you just saw rather than jumping randomly across files. A Basic realm helps explain the authentication challenge, but it does not decide whether the submitted credentials are correct.
lessons.38: Now move from storefront customers to the older services section. Before protecting a service URL, where do its users come from? Read this adapter's authentication `configure()`. We place it here because it's the services counterpart to Company 35. Compare the identity source instead of assuming the same customer service powers every application endpoint.
lessons.39: Having an identity source isn't enough. Should a public service endpoint and a private service operation be treated alike? Open the next service `configure()` chain and inspect its URL rules. This follows Company 38 as the authorization half of the story. Trace which patterns are open and which require authentication; one broad pattern can overshadow a more specific one.
lessons.40: You saw the services rules use a Basic authentication entry point. Let's find `servicesAuthenticationEntryPoint()` and see how it supplies the challenge. We study it now because Company 39 references this factory directly. Comparing the service realm to the shop realm helps beginners see that even similar authentication mechanisms can belong to different client entry points.
lessons.41: We are now leaving the legacy service flow and entering administrator JWT security. Open the admin adapter's `authenticationManagerBean()`. Notice we skip a commented-out adapter section; commented source isn't active configuration. This is the first admin step because it exposes the manager that later admin provider and routing rules use. Think of keeping the staff entrance separate from the shopper entrance.
lessons.42: How does an admin login get checked? The authentication manager needs a provider and user lookup. Inspect this adapter's `configure()` and the dependency it registers. We place it after Company 41 because exposing a manager and configuring how it authenticates are distinct responsibilities. Pay attention to admin-specific classes; customer credentials should not accidentally be accepted as administrator credentials.
lessons.43: While designing admin API security, you might need documentation routes such as Swagger to remain accessible. Open the web-security `configure()` that excludes the documented UI path. We inspect this before private admin routes so you can tell an ignored path from an allowed request. The presence of Swagger does not mean every admin operation should be public.
lessons.44: Now for the serious part: which administrator API requests are protected? Open the admin HttpSecurity `configure()` method and read the matcher chain. This comes after provider setup and Swagger exclusions because we can now evaluate authentication and authorization together. Imagine a back-office inventory operation accidentally covered by a permissive URL matcher—checking the real paths matters.
lessons.45: The admin configuration calls a provider factory. Instead of guessing what the provider does, follow `authenticationProvider()` and find the concrete instance it builds. This comes after the admin rule chain because you now know why that provider is needed. Later, Company 54 opens its `authenticate()` implementation so we can audit the actual credential checks.
lessons.46: The admin API uses HTTP Basic in one part of its configuration. Where is the actual challenge entry point prepared? Follow `apiAdminAuthenticationEntryPoint()` from Company 44. We place it here so the method call in the security chain has a concrete destination. A realm tells the client what kind of login is expected; the password still needs checking somewhere else.
lessons.47: Imagine the same Shopizer server accepts both staff and customer API calls. Should they share one authentication manager without distinction? Let's enter the customer JWT adapter through `authenticationManagerBean()`. This comes after admin security because the side-by-side comparison becomes much clearer. Watch the adapter order and the specific security chain rather than relying on the word 'JWT' alone.
lessons.48: The customer JWT manager exists. Now who supplies its user details? Inspect the customer authentication `configure()` method. We study this before URL rules so we know where the authenticated identity comes from. Picture a shopper signing in with an email and password: this provider's identity source must resolve the correct customer, not the administrator account from the previous section.
lessons.49: Suppose a customer requests a token or calls an account endpoint. Which requests require authentication, and which endpoints are used to obtain it? Open the customer HttpSecurity `configure()` rules. We put this after identity configuration so you can read the whole chain, from recognizing a user to deciding access. Check the literal matchers; an overly broad pattern is a security bug, not a shortcut.
lessons.50: We have customer API rules, but the chain still needs someone to validate credentials. Follow `authenticationProvider()` and see the customer provider factory. This is the companion to the admin provider in Company 45. The important question is which concrete class gets constructed: the answer tells us which authentication logic to inspect next, not just which interface it implements.
lessons.51: When a customer API request has no acceptable credentials, the application needs a proper challenge. Open `apiCustomerAuthenticationEntryPoint()`. We study this right after the customer provider so the success and rejection pathways stay together in your mind. Compare the realm and response behavior with the admin entry point; identical-looking APIs don't necessarily have identical access policies.
lessons.52: Let's stop looking at configuration and watch a real request arrive. `doFilterInternal()` is where this authentication filter handles the current HTTP request. Follow how it extracts or processes authentication information, then continues the filter chain. We arrive here after wiring all the security entry points so the earlier factories finally connect to executable behavior. A filter must not forget to pass eligible requests onward.
lessons.53: Company 52 runs during a request. But when that request finishes, what happens to thread-local or security-related context? Open `postFilter()` and review the cleanup. We place this directly after the main filter because leaving request state behind can contaminate the next request on a reused worker thread. This is one of those quiet production bugs that a happy-path test might miss.
lessons.54: Now follow the administrator provider we built in Company 45. Open its `authenticate()` method and imagine a staff member trying to sign in. Where is the user loaded? What token is returned, and what happens when credentials fail? This method belongs here because we already know who constructed the provider. Don't assume the authentication is secure until you've inspected its password verification path.
lessons.55: A login method can look convincing until you inspect how it checks passwords. Open `passwordMatch()`, the helper used by Company 54, and compare its actual logic with BCrypt-style verification. This is intentionally next because credential comparison is too important to hide behind a method name. The teaching lesson is to distinguish what the method promises from what the source truly enforces.
lessons.56: If Spring has more than one authentication provider, how does it know which provider can handle a given token type? Find `supports(Class<?>)`. We study it after the password helper because now you understand authentication decisions and can examine provider selection. Supporting a class doesn't automatically mean a particular login will succeed; it only says this provider is a candidate.
lessons.57: We've seen how an administrator authenticates. A shopper should have a separate path, so open the customer provider's `authenticate()`. Compare the steps with Company 54: which identity service is called, what exceptions can happen, and what principal is produced? We put these methods next to each other so you learn by comparison rather than memorizing two isolated classes.
lessons.58: Don't stop at the customer provider's happy path. Just as with admin login, the password helper is where assumptions can break. Inspect `passwordMatch()` in the customer provider and compare its exact expression to Company 55. This is the second half of that authentication story: identifying a customer is different from proving the supplied password matches.
lessons.59: A provider can contain authentication code and still never be chosen for the wrong token type. Let's inspect customer `supports()`. We study this after password comparison because the whole provider contract now has three pieces: selection, credential check, and result. Compare its supported class with Company 56 before assuming a customer login could safely flow through the admin provider.
lessons.60: We've finished the main customer provider behavior. What user-details service has been attached to this object? Open `getJwtCustomerDetailsService()`. We place the accessor here to expose the dependency behind the provider's identity lookup. An accessor returning a field doesn't create a service; the important follow-up is how that field was injected and whether it is correctly configured.
lessons.61: Now pair that getter with `setJwtCustomerDetailsService()`. Imagine a test trying to replace the provider's identity loader with a fake implementation. A setter changes the local field, but does that also configure anything inherited from Spring Security? We study this after Company 60 so field ownership is visible. Inspect the assignment rather than treating all setters as equivalent framework wiring.
lessons.62: We're moving into JWT tokens. First question: who does this token say it belongs to? Open `getUsernameFromToken()` and look at the subject claim. That's our entry point into `JWTTokenUtil` because identity must be understood before expiry, audience, or refresh. Remember that reading a claim from an untrusted string and verifying a signed token are different security steps.
lessons.63: A token names a user, but we also need to know when it was issued. Inspect `getIssuedAtDateFromToken()`. We study issuance immediately after username because timing affects password-reset and token-revocation checks later. Think of a ticket stamped at a concert entrance: the timestamp helps answer whether the ticket predates a security event.
lessons.64: Suppose someone saved a token from last week. Can it still be used? Open `getExpirationDateFromToken()` and see where its expiry claim comes from. This comes after issue time because the two dates tell different stories. The expiry value is evidence for a later decision; merely reading it doesn't enforce a rejection without an actual comparison.
lessons.65: We know the user and the dates. Now who is the token intended for? Step into `getAudienceFromToken()`. This belongs after expiry because we're completing the basic claim vocabulary before evaluating tokens. A mobile app and a web browser might be treated differently by the surrounding code, but the audience claim alone does not prove a client can be trusted.
lessons.66: Notice how several JWT getters look almost identical. Do we really want each one to parse the token from scratch? Open `getClaimFromToken()`, the generic helper they share. This comes after the individual getters so you recognize the repetition it removes. The callback selects one claim, while the token parser performs another job. Learning this separation makes the next method much easier.
lessons.67: Now let's open the box rather than just ask for individual labels. `getAllClaimsFromToken()` is where the JWT is parsed and its signature-handling configuration is applied. We follow the generic helper down to its core dependency. This is the critical security boundary: a claim is trustworthy only after the library has successfully validated the token under the intended signing rules.
lessons.68: We can read the `exp` claim. How do we actually reject an expired ticket? Inspect `isTokenExpired()` and follow the date comparison. This comes after parsing because validation depends on the expiry we just extracted. Look for edge cases around equality and time zones; dates are not just strings, and a strict check has specific boundary behavior.
lessons.69: What happens when servers and client clocks disagree by a few seconds? Shopizer has `isTokenExpiredWithGrace()`, which uses a 200-second allowance. We put it right after the strict check so you can see exactly what changes. A grace period can help with clock skew, but it also extends a token's practical acceptance window. That's a conscious security trade-off.
lessons.70: Imagine a customer changes their password after a token was issued. Should the older token still work? Open `isCreatedBeforeLastPasswordReset()` and examine the timestamp comparison. We learn this after expiration because a token can be unexpired yet still need revocation. This is the bridge between token metadata and real account-security events.
lessons.71: Company 70 used a strict password-reset cutoff. Now `isCreatedBeforeLastPasswordResetWithGrace()` adjusts that comparison by 200 seconds. We study it immediately to compare both policies with the same mental example: a token issued just before a password change. A shifted cutoff can be more forgiving, but the source—not the method's friendly name—determines whether it weakens revocation.
lessons.72: Those grace checks mention seconds, so where does the date arithmetic happen? Open `addSeconds()`. We place this tiny helper here because you've just seen two callers that need it. Pay attention to the conversion from seconds to timestamp units; a harmless-looking multiplication can change token acceptance by orders of magnitude if the units are wrong.
lessons.73: We've learned how to read and evaluate JWT claims. Now let's build a new token, starting with whom it's for. Inspect `generateAudience()` and the value it chooses. This comes before token signing because we should understand the claims going into the token before examining the final signed result. The audience is part of the token's meaning, not just decoration.
lessons.74: One method in this file makes special decisions about expiration for particular audiences. Open `ignoreTokenExpiration()` and review the conditions for mobile and tablet clients. We study it after audience generation so the condition has context. This is also a useful security-review question: any bypass of expiry, however intentional, deserves a very clear policy and tests.
lessons.75: Enough preparation—how does Shopizer ask for a new JWT? Open `generateToken()`. We put the public entry point after the claim helpers because its parameters now have meaning. Follow what data it collects and which private builder it calls next. Think of writing the contents of a boarding pass before placing the tamper-evident seal on it.
lessons.76: Company 75 hands token creation to `doGenerateToken()`. Here's where the actual signing operation happens, using the source's HS512 configuration. We study this method now because the token's security rests on both its claims and its signing key. Don't confuse encoding a JWT with encrypting its contents; signed payloads may still be readable.
lessons.77: Creating a token is one thing; deciding whether it may be refreshed is another. Open `canTokenBeRefreshedWithGrace()`. Pay close attention if the source returns a constant rather than evaluating the expected conditions. We placed this after token signing because refresh is a new lifecycle stage. This is an audit moment: a reassuring method name cannot substitute for a real eligibility check.
lessons.78: Compare that grace-based refresh method with `canTokenBeRefreshed()`. This time trace the boolean expression and its expiry/reset checks. We study them back-to-back to show why two nearly identical API names can encode very different behavior. In a real incident, checking which method a caller actually uses is just as important as reading its implementation.
lessons.79: Suppose a valid session needs a fresh JWT. Does the app invent a new identity or reuse existing claims? Open `refreshToken()` and inspect the reissue steps. This follows the eligibility checks: first decide whether refresh should be allowed, then see what the refresh operation actually does. Watch the new issue and expiry timestamps; copying an old payload blindly has security consequences.
lessons.80: Now gather the pieces together. `validateToken()` checks whether a token belongs to the expected user and passes the relevant time/password-reset rules. We place it here after claims, expiry, refresh, and signing because you can finally explain the combined decision instead of memorizing a single boolean. A token may be correctly signed yet inappropriate for the current account state.
lessons.81: Before leaving JWT utilities, one last helper controls when new tokens expire: `calculateExpirationDate()`. Open it and follow the timestamp arithmetic. This finishes the generation story by connecting configuration to the `exp` claim. Remember to ask whether the time unit is milliseconds, seconds, or something else; token-duration bugs often start with an innocent-looking number.
lessons.82: Let's move from the JWT utility to the request-authentication manager. Where does it look for the incoming token? Inspect `getTokenHeader()`. We start here because you can't validate credentials you haven't located. A header name is merely configuration: it tells the application where to look, not whether the value in that header is trustworthy.
lessons.83: Someone may need to configure a different header name in a test or deployment. Open `setTokenHeader()` and see how the value is stored. We place this directly after the getter to understand the little piece of mutable state the manager depends on. Changing a configured header affects request parsing, but it does not automatically change the underlying authentication rules.
lessons.84: Now imagine a request arriving with that header. What coordinates the whole login attempt? Step into `authenticateRequest()` and trace the decision paths. This comes after the header accessors because we've learned the input location before the workflow. Observe how the manager calls authentication logic and chooses success or failure handling—don't assume every nonempty token is valid.
lessons.85: Company 84 found an authenticated result. Where should that identity live for the rest of the request? Open `success()` and inspect how it updates Spring's security context. We study this immediately after the main workflow because setting context is a separate, security-sensitive action. The goal is for downstream code to see the right principal—never a stale one from another request.
lessons.86: What if the same authentication attempt fails? A previous user context must not remain lying around. Examine `unsuccess()` and its cleanup behavior. We pair it with Company 85 so you see both sides of the context lifecycle. Imagine a pooled server thread accidentally retaining one shopper's identity when the next request is rejected; this method is part of preventing that sort of leak.
lessons.87: When someone calls a protected REST endpoint without valid authentication, what should the API return? Open `commence()` in `RestAuthenticationEntryPoint.java`. We place the REST entry point after manager success/failure because it's the HTTP-facing rejection path. A clear 401 response tells the client authentication is required; it is not a substitute for authorization checks after login.
lessons.88: Multiple entry points can compete for a request, so how does one declare its order? Look at `getOrder()` in the REST entry point. This comes right after the 401 response because we want to understand not only what the handler does, but when a framework may select it. Compare the actual numeric priority with the service entry point you'll see shortly.
lessons.89: Before a REST authentication entry point serves traffic, should its required settings be missing? Inspect `afterPropertiesSet()`. We study startup validation after response and ordering because these three methods form one complete component: behavior, selection, and initialization. Catching bad configuration early can be much easier than discovering it as a confusing 401 in production.
lessons.90: A service client can also be rejected, but its challenge may be configured separately from a REST browser or API flow. Open the service `commence()` and compare the exact response with Company 87. This side-by-side lesson is deliberate: matching interface names do not guarantee identical settings. Notice the response status and headers rather than inferring them from the class name.
lessons.91: The service entry point can answer with 401, but which one takes precedence when several ordered handlers exist? Check its `getOrder()` and compare it with Company 88. We're doing this after the service response so priority has a concrete meaning. A smaller ordering value generally means higher precedence for ordered components, but always check the framework's selection rules.
lessons.92: Before this service entry point is used, its realm or other required settings may need validation. Open `afterPropertiesSet()` and inspect the actual guard. We finish the service entry point here because a component should be understood from setup through failure response. A missing property should produce an understandable startup issue instead of silently affecting authentication challenges.
lessons.93: We've studied what happens when a service caller is refused. Now imagine successful authentication: does the service need to replay a saved browser request? Open `onAuthenticationSuccess()` and examine how Shopizer deals with request state. We place it after the failure-entry-point sequence to compare rejected requests with accepted ones. A service integration may behave very differently from an interactive storefront login.
lessons.94: Company 93 works with a request cache. Who supplies that cache? See `setRequestCache()` and its assignment. We study the setter after the success callback because now you know why the field matters. A cache used for saved requests is not automatically a data cache for products or customers, so don't confuse the two just because both use the word 'cache'.
lessons.95: Let's move from HTTP entry points into finding customer identities. How does the customer service get access to customers, groups, and permissions? Open the `AbstractCustomerServices` constructor and follow the three injected collaborators. We begin here because a login lookup cannot work without its data sources. Notice that this is constructor wiring, not yet the actual username search.
lessons.96: Imagine a shopper enters a username. Shopizer has to load the matching customer and assemble that person's granted authorities. Follow `loadUserByUsername()` from the dependencies we just wired in Company 95. Watch the missing-user path and the group/permission aggregation. This is the heart of identity lookup; credentials still need separate verification by an authentication provider.
lessons.97: The abstract service defines common lookup behavior, but a real browser login needs a concrete subclass. Open the `CustomerServicesImpl` constructor to see which services it forwards to the base class. This follows Company 96 so inheritance feels practical: the subclass can reuse one lookup workflow while customizing how the returned principal is built.
lessons.98: Company 96 has found a customer. What should Spring Security receive as the authenticated principal? Open `userDetails()` in `CustomerServicesImpl` and watch the `CustomerDetails` object being filled. We put this right after the subclass constructor because it's the concrete result of the inherited lookup. Notice which fields are copied from trusted customer data, not from arbitrary request parameters.
lessons.99: Social login often looks like a separate feature, but should we duplicate all the customer lookup code? See what `SocialCustomerServicesImpl.loadUserByUsername()` actually delegates to. We study it after the browser service to compare reuse with implementation. A social identity still has to be connected to a real customer account; delegation alone doesn't prove a provider verified the social token.
lessons.100: Now introduce JWT-specific customer lookup. Open the `JWTCustomerServicesImpl` constructor and trace its inherited dependencies. This is our bridge from browser/social principals to API bearer-token principals. The underlying customer may be the same, but the resulting `UserDetails` type and authentication flow can be different. Constructor wiring helps explain where that identity data originates.
lessons.101: The inherited lookup has a JWT-specific implementation hook. Open `userDetails()` in `JWTCustomerServicesImpl` and see how it constructs a `JWTUser`. We place it here after wiring because you can follow a resolved customer into the principal used by token authentication. Look carefully at any hard-coded account flags; source code can say 'enabled' even when business rules might disagree.
lessons.102: The customer JWT principal makes sense. How does an administrator principal get built? Compare the admin `userDetails()` with Company 101. We're learning by contrast: administrative groups and authorities have stronger security implications than an ordinary shopping account. Confirm what data is copied and what checks are actually performed, rather than assuming a principal named 'admin' automatically has privileges.
lessons.103: Company 102 builds an administrator principal, but where do its user and permissions come from? Open the admin `loadUserByUsername()`. We study the lookup after the builder so you can work backward from the principal to the source records. Trace missing-user behavior and group authority construction, especially because incorrect permission aggregation could open a back-office endpoint to the wrong user.
lessons.104: We know how to build customer JWT identities. Let's see how a bearer token is authenticated on an actual request. Open `attemptAuthentication()` in the customer manager. This comes after user lookup so each validation step has a destination. Check how the token is extracted, which user gets loaded, and which claims are compared; reading a username is not the same as trusting the whole token.
lessons.105: What happens immediately after the customer JWT manager says authentication succeeded? Inspect `successfullAuthentication()`—including the method's original spelling. We study the hook after Company 104 so its place in the workflow is clear. The source may leave this callback empty, and that's a fact worth noticing: never invent side effects just because a callback has an important name.
lessons.106: Now imagine the bearer token is rejected. Open `unSuccessfullAuthentication()` and compare it with the success hook. We place these two callbacks side by side to make failure handling explicit. If the override contains no statements, say so; any real cleanup might live elsewhere, such as the base authentication manager. A blank method still teaches us about extension points.
lessons.107: Admin JWT authentication deserves its own review. Compare `JWTAdminAuthenticationManager.attemptAuthentication()` with the customer version in Company 104. We study it after finishing the customer callbacks because the flow is familiar but the identity and privileges are different. Follow the specific admin lookup and token validation; staff access should never be inferred from a token's self-declared username alone.
lessons.108: Where does the admin manager go after a successful token check? Open its `successfullAuthentication()` hook and compare it with Company 105. We place it here to see whether admin and customer flows add different post-login work. If the body is empty, that is the lesson: framework hooks are optional extension points, not guarantees of a particular response or audit log.
lessons.109: Let's finish the admin manager's other side: `unSuccessfullAuthentication()`. We've seen the success hook, so now examine the failure override and whether it does any real work. This closes the comparison with the customer manager. A method can exist for symmetry or future customization while doing nothing today; accurate code reading starts by acknowledging that.
lessons.110: We've spent time on bearer tokens. Now return to plain credential rules: what if a merchant chooses a weak password or the confirmation doesn't match? Open `validateCredentials()` and trace its checks. We study it here to distinguish account-password validation from JWT signing and bearer-token verification. Each layer protects a different part of the login story.
lessons.111: The credentials service also declares `generatePassword()`. Does that mean the system has a working password generator? Open the body and judge it from its implementation. We place this after credential validation so you can compare a finished rule with an incomplete feature. A stub or unsupported operation must never be presented to a student as production-ready password generation.
lessons.112: Our browser-login service created `CustomerDetails` earlier. What's inside that principal when it is constructed? Open its full constructor and inspect the flags and authorities passed to Spring Security's `User` superclass. This comes after authentication workflows because you now understand why Spring needs these properties. Distinguish the customer's real account state from values the constructor receives.
lessons.113: The JWT services created `JWTUser`, so let's finally inspect its constructor. Imagine packing a secure identity card: which fields go on it, and which remain internal? We study this after the browser principal to compare two representations of authenticated users. The constructor stores data; it doesn't itself verify signatures or compare passwords.
lessons.114: Spring Security needs to access a principal's password value during certain authentication flows. Open `JWTUser.getPassword()` and inspect the simple return. We place it after the constructor because you now know where the stored field came from. A password getter should never be mistaken for a password-verification routine, and exposing credentials through JSON would be a separate hazard.
lessons.115: An authenticated user is more than a username; Spring may need the roles or authorities the principal carries. Look at `getAuthorities()`. We study it after the password accessor because identity and permissions are separate pieces of `UserDetails`. Ask where those authorities were originally populated, especially when comparing customer and administrator roles.
lessons.116: What if a customer resets their password and an older JWT is still circulating? Open `getLastPasswordResetDate()`, the field accessor used by the token validation rules. We place it after the principal's other security properties so the link to Company 80 becomes visible. This getter only supplies the date; the actual token-revocation decision occurs in another method.
lessons.117: Let's finish the `JWTUser` properties we haven't visited yet, starting with `getId()`. Imagine two customers changing usernames but keeping their database identities. That's why a stable ID matters. Inspect the `@JsonIgnore` annotation as well: making an internal field available to Java code doesn't mean we want Jackson to include it in every API response.
lessons.118: Now compare that internal ID with `getUsername()`. Spring Security asks `UserDetails` for the principal's login name, not necessarily the database's primary key. We study this after Company 117 so the distinction is fresh. Imagine someone renaming an account; how would your code preserve identity if authorization mistakenly depended on the mutable username?
lessons.119: Does Shopizer's `JWTUser` actually expire an account? Open `isAccountNonExpired()` and read the return value instead of trusting its name. We place this first among three account-state checks because expiration is easy to picture: an account valid yesterday may be invalid today. If the source always returns true, another layer would need to enforce a real expiry policy.
lessons.120: An account can still be valid in time but locked because of abuse. Visit `isAccountNonLocked()` and compare it with Company 119. We study it second to show these booleans represent different policies. Picture a shopper with too many failed attempts: if this method always reports unlocked, the lockout decision must happen somewhere else—or it may not happen at all.
lessons.121: A password can expire even when the account itself is healthy. Check `isCredentialsNonExpired()` as the third state flag. We place it after account expiry and lock status so you won't collapse three distinct rules into one 'user enabled' switch. If the method returns a constant true, document that reality and ask where credential rotation is actually enforced.
lessons.122: We've finished the account-status checks. Now let's look at display information carried in `JWTUser`. Start with `getFirstname()`. This comes after the security booleans because a profile name is useful to the UI but should not be confused with authentication identity. Check whether Jackson can serialize the value and whether the application really needs to expose it.
lessons.123: A customer may change their surname without changing their login. Open `getLastname()` and compare it with the first-name accessor. We put this next because together they form display data, not permission rules. The method is simple, but the design lesson is important: names are not unique, immutable, or safe identifiers for authorization.
lessons.124: Email is even more interesting: users expect to receive messages there, but an email can change and might be unverified. Look at `JWTUser.getEmail()`. This follows the name fields so you can separate profile/contact data from stable account identity. Don't interpret a returned email value as proof that its owner has verified that address.
lessons.125: Before leaving `JWTUser`, inspect `isEnabled()`. Unlike some of the earlier constant account-state getters, this one returns a stored flag. We study it last to tie the security contract back to the constructors and JWT principal builders. Look for any caller that always passes true; the presence of a boolean field doesn't guarantee a real disabled-account policy.
lessons.126: Switch from JWT principals back to the browser version. The three-argument `CustomerDetails` constructor is shorter than the full constructor in Company 112. What values does it supply behind the scenes? Open it and inspect the `super(...)` call. We place it here to highlight default account-state flags: a convenient constructor can also conceal security assumptions.
lessons.127: Now inspect the extra email field on the browser's `CustomerDetails` principal. Open `getEmail()`. We learn this getter before its setter because first we ask what data other code can read. Email is useful for communication, but remember it is not necessarily the username or a stable customer key.
lessons.128: Company 98 fills in browser-principal details after constructing the object. Which method receives the customer email? Follow `setEmail()` and the assignment it performs. This comes directly after the getter so you can connect reading and writing the same piece of state. A mutable principal is convenient, but changing it after authentication can make session state drift from the database.
lessons.129: After email, look at the more stable `CustomerDetails` ID. Open `getId()` and see the value returned. We study it after the email pair because you can now compare a contact address with a database identity. Imagine two users trading email addresses: their customer records still need distinct IDs.
lessons.130: Where does that ID come from when Shopizer prepares the browser principal? Open `setId()` and follow its call from Company 98. We put it right after `getId()` to close the data flow: source customer record → principal field → later lookup. The important security lesson is to copy IDs from trusted backend objects, not untrusted form values.
lessons.131: Our principal also carries a friendly first name. Read `getFirstName()` after the email and ID accessors. This isn't a login credential; it's display information a page might show after sign-in. We study it here so beginners see how one authenticated principal can carry both security identity and optional profile fields without mixing their purposes.
lessons.132: How is that friendly name updated in memory? Open `setFirstName()` and see the assignment. We place it after the getter to make the mutability obvious. Notice that the browser-principal creation method we inspected doesn't necessarily call this setter; don't invent a caller when the source hasn't shown one. A setter's existence is not evidence that every login populates it.
lessons.133: Let's finish the display profile with `getLastName()`. We already know how the first name is read; now find the surname field. This comes here because both values often appear together in the user interface, but neither should control account permissions. A name returned from a principal may be stale if the customer edited their profile during a long-lived session.
lessons.134: The last browser-profile setter is `setLastName()`. Read its one assignment and compare it with Company 132. We study it after the getter because you can see the complete read/write pair for a mutable field. The interesting question isn't whether Java can assign a string; it's how an authenticated session stays consistent when profile data changes.
lessons.135: Now revisit administrator authentication with the principal concepts fresh in mind. Open `getJwtAdminDetailsService()` inside the admin provider. It returns a user-details service field used in that component's wiring. We place this near the end because you've already seen the admin authentication logic in Company 54; now we're inspecting the small accessors that support it.
lessons.136: Let's close this batch with the matching `setJwtAdminDetailsService()`. Imagine swapping in a test identity service: the setter changes a field on this subclass, but does that also configure the inherited Spring authentication provider? We study it after Company 135 to make that subtle distinction clear. One assignment is not proof that framework-level wiring has changed correctly.
lessons.137: Imagine a shopper opening our login page. The browser will send a username and password, but Java needs an object to receive them. Find `AuthenticationRequest()` and notice it just calls `super()`. That is why we start here: creating request data is different from proving identity. Neither a database lookup nor a password check occurs in this constructor. Authentication will be handled by the controller and security manager.
lessons.138: To reproduce a login case in a unit test, we can create an `AuthenticationRequest` with two arguments. Open this constructor and follow its calls to `setUsername()` and `setPassword()`. Those are assignments, not authorization decisions. We study the convenient constructor after the empty one because both create the same input shape in different ways. The supplied password still needs authentication by a provider.
lessons.139: A returning customer types an email address and clicks Sign in. `getUsername()` returns the account name held in the incoming request, and the controller can send that value to an authentication manager. But it is still just user-submitted text. Do not confuse it with a username obtained from a successfully authenticated principal. This distinction protects us from treating arbitrary client claims as trusted customer identity.
lessons.140: Where does the username in the request JSON go? `setUsername()` simply assigns a String field. The `@NotEmpty` annotation attached to that field can reject empty input when Bean Validation runs, but the assignment doesn't enforce account ownership. A nonempty username may still be unknown or malicious. We put this after the getter so you can see the complete data path before the application attempts authentication.
lessons.141: Now follow the password. The login controller calls `getPassword()` to obtain the value the shopper submitted, then passes it to the authentication machinery. This getter neither hashes nor compares anything. That's not a bug by itself; the request class is only a carrier. What would be dangerous is logging the returned secret or assuming it has already been checked. Keep the verification in the proper security layer.
lessons.142: A customer enters a password and the JSON binder needs a field to hold it. `setPassword()` does exactly that and nothing else. The nearby `@NotEmpty` constraint checks missing input only when validation is invoked; it doesn't compare credentials. Understanding this tiny method helps prevent the common mistake of confusing request-body population with a successful login. The raw value is sensitive and should not be printed or retained unnecessarily.
lessons.143: Once login succeeds, the frontend expects a response rather than a Java authentication object. Start with the no-argument `AuthenticationResponse()` constructor. It doesn't generate a token, set a customer ID, or check expiry. We study this tiny method so you can see that a response object is a container, not a JWT issuer. The next constructor shows exactly where an already-generated token and customer ID are placed.
lessons.144: Picture the login response as an envelope containing the customer's ID and the server-issued JWT. `AuthenticationResponse(Long userId, String token)` stores the token field and forwards the ID to `super.setId(userId)`. That ID lives in the superclass, not a newly declared field here. Notice that no cryptographic signing happens in this constructor. The security utility must have issued the token before the response is assembled.
lessons.145: The storefront needs to receive the token after a successful login. `getToken()` returns the value held in the response object. It's not refreshing the session, verifying a signature or checking permissions. That simplicity matters: we can reason about where the token comes from without hiding complex behavior in a property getter. With both request and response models understood, we're ready to visit the actual controller that connects them.
lessons.146: A first-time shopper submits the registration form. In `/customer/register`, notice that Shopizer copies email into username, checks for an existing account, requires billing details and registers through CustomerFacade. It then authenticates the credentials, reloads the JWT principal and generates a token for the response. This is more than saving a user record. One caution: the catch block returns 404 on authentication exceptions, which is a confusing error status.
lessons.147: Most customers register once and log in many times. Open `/customer/login`: the controller reads our request's username and password and passes a `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken` to the authentication manager. On success, it sets the security context, loads a `JWTUser`, generates a JWT and returns an `AuthenticationResponse`. The token object representing submitted credentials is not automatically trusted. Observe the distinct failure responses: 401 for bad credentials and 500 for other exceptions.
lessons.148: Imagine someone leaving a shopping cart open while their token ages. Should the server issue another token automatically? `refreshToken()` reads the configured header, extracts the subject, reloads the principal and consults `canTokenBeRefreshed()` using the last password reset date. Only an eligible token is refreshed and sent in a new response. The short handler should not be mistaken for comprehensive validation of every malformed or compromised token case.
lessons.149: A shopper wants to replace their password. Before accepting the new one, the system should check that they know the existing credential. `PasswordRequest` extends `AuthenticationRequest` and adds `current`; `getCurrent()` supplies that value to the later controller. This accessor doesn't check the password itself. The facade performs the comparison. We learn it now to distinguish confirming the old secret from confirming that the new secret was typed consistently.
lessons.150: The password-change form has a Current password field. `setCurrent()` assigns whatever String arrived. The adjacent `@NotEmpty` constraint can reject missing input when validation runs, but it cannot prove the value matches the account's password. We're studying this modest setter because it's easy to give simple code too much credit. A proper account update must still compare the supplied old password with stored credentials before making changes.
lessons.151: A customer types their replacement password twice to catch typing mistakes. The second value is read through `getRepeatPassword()`, while the new password itself comes from the inherited `getPassword()`. An equality check reduces accidental mismatches; it doesn't prove the old credential was correct and doesn't guarantee password strength. Keeping these separate helps us design specific validation messages and avoid overlooking a required security check.
lessons.152: Look at the Confirm new password box in our storefront. `setRepeatPassword()` is the place where Java stores that submitted value. It does not compare it with the proposed password; the controller does so later. This division lets us tell apart missing confirmation, mismatched new values and an incorrect current credential. All three errors might surface during one operation, but each arises from a different rule.
lessons.153: Now follow `/auth/customer/password`. The API finds the merchant, loads a customer by the submitted username, checks the current password, compares new and repeated passwords, then calls `customerFacade.changePassword()`. Each condition addresses a different risk. The catch block returns `e.getMessage()` to the client, potentially disclosing internal details. Also question how the caller is tied to the target account; client-supplied username alone must not grant permission to change it.
lessons.154: Suppose an administrator asks what the Inventory Manager group can do. `/private/{group}/permissions` finds a named group and converts its Permission objects into readable names and IDs. We're moving from authentication, who is logged in, to authorization, what they can access. Spot the catch block: it catches Exception after a ResourceNotFoundException can be thrown, obscuring the intended not-found error. The endpoint teaches both group mapping and careful error handling.
lessons.155: Imagine building an admin settings page that lists every possible permission. `permissions()` calls `permissionService.list()` and converts each result into `ReadablePermission` with an ID and name. Unlike Company 154, this does not filter by group. Notice that the shown method has no pagination logic, which matters when catalogs grow. Also a URL containing `/private/` is just a path string, not proof that the endpoint is protected by Spring Security.
lessons.156: An admin interface often needs a list of available groups or roles. Open `groups()` and follow `groupService.list()`: the handler creates one `ReadableGroup` per result and copies its name, ID and group type. This completes the path from receiving credentials to exploring permissions and groups. But listing groups is not itself authorization; separate Spring Security rules must decide which callers may access this route and administer assignments.
